| [NOTE-130](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-130.md) v2 | Floridi — The Informational Nature of Personal Identity | Floridi deflates the diachronic question of personal identity, holding that sameness is always relative to a purpose-fixed level of abstraction and that metaphysical versions of the question "do not deserve to be taken seriously" (p. 554). He puts the synchronic question first: what binds a self's information into a unity. His answer is an admittedly "figurative" 3C model in which the self is the last of three successive encapsulations, corporeal (bonded by chemical bonds), cognitive (bonded by mutual information) and conscious (bonded by semantics, and so dependent on a community). He then reads ICTs as "egopoietic" technologies because they act on all three membranes. | Read |
| [NOTE-180](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-180.md) v4 | Clark & Chalmers — The Extended Mind | The paper argues from a functionalist parity claim that a process or standing state which would count as cognitive if it happened in the head counts as cognitive when an external resource carries it, provided the resource is actively coupled to the organism here and now. Otto's notebook entry is its example of such a standing belief. From this it infers, in one paragraph, that the self extends too. The four "criteria" for a coupled resource (constancy, direct availability, automatic endorsement, and the admittedly "arguable" past conscious endorsement) are offered as the features that make the paradigm case clear. The paper explicitly says they are not necessary and sufficient conditions. | Read |
| [NOTE-264](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-264.md) | I. Taking Ourselves Seriously; II. Getting It Right | Frankfurt grounds practical reason and normativity in the will rather than in reason. Reflexive self-division makes higher-order attitudes possible (pp. 170–171). Identification, a largely default "willing acceptance" (p. 173), turns a desire from "a problem" into a reason (p. 175). Free will is "volitional unanimity" between the governing desire and higher-order volitions (p. 177), and caring is wanting to go on wanting (p. 180). Final ends and their normative authority come from love, "strictly volitional" (p. 196): its involuntary, wholehearted "volitional necessities" are "irresistible, but … not coercive" (p. 197) and are "the only legitimate authority" for our normative convictions (p. 201). The 1971 wanton/person taxonomy is gestured at in a single phrase and its apparatus is not restated. | Read |
| [NOTE-268](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-268.md) | Identification and Identity | Velleman targets Frankfurt's *later* conception of autonomy. On that conception, a person acts autonomously only when his volitions derive from "the essential character of his will", and that essence consists of volitional necessities that are also the conditions of his personal identity. Velleman argues against it on three grounds. Such an essence would ground authenticity, not autonomy (the Winnicottian False Self is inauthentic but over-controlled). Frankfurt offers no argument or example that motivational change ends a person. And the ideal of wholeheartedness, which cures ambivalence by extruding a desire from the self, is a defensive fantasy: Freud's Rat Man was made ill by just such a separation, and identifying with part of oneself in the ordinary, imaginative sense is Sartrean bad faith. He replaces "the self" with an *aspectual* reading of "self" as a marker of reflexivity. On that reading autonomy is behaviour motivated partly by the understanding, the part of us "with which we cannot help identifying", without its being our identity (pp. 357–360). | Read |
| [NOTE-338](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-338.md) | Where Am I? | A first-person story with an argument inside. With his brain in a vat in Houston radio-linked to his body under Tulsa, the narrator tests three answers to "where am I?": where the body is, where the brain is, where the point of view is. He favours the third and finds it unclear. A computer duplicate of his brain can take over his body with no detectable difference, and when duplicate and brain drift out of step there are two persons in one body. Intuition pumps, no thesis defended to the end. | Read |
| [NOTE-341](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-341.md) | The Computational Boundary of a "Self" | A hypothesis essay. A Self is the set of parts that pursue goals together, and its boundary is the farthest region of space and time it can measure and act on, its "cognitive light cone". Selves grow from homeostatic loops by adding memory, anticipation and networks, and cells form larger Selves by sharing bioelectric state through gap junctions. Every level that has its own goal is a Self, so living systems hold many nested Selves at once; the paper says this against IIT in one bracket. It has no model, no measurement of the light cone and no new data, and it confines claims about experience to a closing speculation. | Read |
| [NOTE-348](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-348.md) | The Emotion Machine | Read in the 2005 draft. Emotions are Ways to Think: each emotional state is a selection of mental resources turned on and off, made by Selectors that Critics trigger when they recognise a type of problem, and ordinary thinking uses the same switching. On this design sit six levels of mental activity, panalogies that link descriptions across realms, and a Self that is a network of partial models. It is argued by example and analogy, with no experiment and few neural claims. Against Damasio, the body is a resource the brain exploits, not what an emotion is made of; on Elliot it proposes, without evidence, the reverse causal direction. | Read |
| [NOTE-364](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-364.md) | The Self as a Center of Narrative Gravity | A self is an abstractum like a centre of gravity, posited by interpretation, and like a fictional character it is indeterminate beyond what its story fixes. A mindless novel-writing robot can author a self whose story is true of the robot. Brains are bundles of partly autonomous systems that make themselves cohere into one autobiography, and when the story coheres around two points there are two selves. The essay argues by analogy and thought experiment. Its evolutionary account of self-talk is speculation, and its evidence is cited. | Read |
| [NOTE-370](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-370.md) | Shanahan, McDonell & Reynolds — Role play with large language models (read for the self) | Read for the self. The simulator has no beliefs, goals or agency, "not even simulated versions"; simulacra only role-play characters that have them, so when an agent says "I" there is "no-one at home". The paper names, and does not answer, the question of which self a dialogue agent would act to preserve: hardware, process or instance. The denial of a self follows from the framing; no argument rules out a conscious actor behind the roles. | Read |
| [NOTE-372](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-372.md) | Self models | Metzinger's compact statement of the self-model theory of subjectivity. No substantial self exists; there is a self-model, partly conscious (the PSM), used for global control. A phenomenal self exists if and only if the PSM is transparent; a first-person perspective is a transparent model of the intentionality relation. Self-models can be unconscious and artificial, and embodiment comes in three orders. The central claim is stated with a prediction, not argued; the examples are cited. The online text has editing slips and reference gaps. | Read |
| [NOTE-376](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-376.md) | Shanahan — Palatable Conceptions of Disembodied Being | An avowedly "poetic" attempt to fit consciousness and selfhood to a disembodied 2024 chat agent. Its time would be discrete and discontinuous. Its "I" can be the model or a conversation-bound self that flickers into being each turn; we may slip between them. Such selves can be copied, edited and merged, and spread over branching simulacra. No candidate site survives scrutiny, which is read as Buddhist emptiness and applied back to human selves. Examples are invented usages, not data. | Read |
| [NOTE-377](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-377.md) | Philosophical conceptions of the self: implications for cognitive science | A short review that sets the minimal self (present self-consciousness) against the narrative self (extended in time), splits the minimal self into a sense of ownership and a sense of agency, and ties their dissociation in schizophrenic thought insertion to Frith's forward comparator model. It reports an embodied minimal self in neonatal imitation and a momentary one in Strawson and in Tani's robot, and proposes, against Dennett, that the narrative self is the sum of its narratives. Evidence is cited, not shown. | Read |
| [NOTE-382](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-382.md) | Shanahan — Simulacra as Conscious Exotica | A Wittgensteinian treatment: consciousness talk is anchored in what is public, so an exotic entity is a candidate only if we could engineer an encounter with it in a shared world. Disembodied chat agents are not candidates; virtually embodied ones could be. On the self: no "self worth preserving" without body, history and autobiographical memory, and no "person behind the mask" for a role player, whose identity is a shifting distribution of roles. Argued by method and scenario; nothing is measured. | Read |
| [NOTE-383](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-383.md) | Against Narrativity | Rejects the descriptive and the normative Narrativity theses. Argues that Episodic lives are normal and can be good, that a from-the-inside memory need not present as one's own, and that self-narration risks falsification. | [NOTE-386](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-386.md) | Of Personal Identity | No impression of a self is constant, so there is no idea of one; introspection finds only perceptions, and the mind is "a bundle or collection of different perceptions". | [NOTE-430](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-430.md) | Relational Frame Theory: Some Implications for Understanding and Treating Human Psychopathology | RFT stated for clinicians. | [NOTE-431](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-431.md) | Acceptance and Commitment Therapy: Model, Processes and Outcomes | The ACT model, read in an early manuscript. Six processes restore flexibility. The manuscript's evidence: AAQ correlations with distress (21 studies), component studies of acceptance and defusion, mediation in seven trials, and weighted outcome effect sizes (d = .49 post and .69 follow-up against active treatments). | Read |
| [NOTE-439](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-439.md) | The "What" and "Why" of Goal Pursuits: Human Needs and the Self-Determination of Behavior | Needs in SDT are innate psychological nutriments, identified functionally by the costs of their thwarting, not by individual differences in their strength. | [NOTE-441](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-441.md) | Self-Regulation and the Problem of Human Autonomy: Does Psychology Need Choice, Self-Determination, and Will? | SDT's autonomy is "regulation by the self": acting with reflective endorsement, graded along the internalization continuum, compatible with external influence, dependence and a single option. Ryan and Deci align it with phenomenological and hierarchical (Frankfurt, Dworkin) accounts and use that definition to answer behaviourist, social-cognitive, reductionist, nonconscious-priming, choice-overload and cultural critiques. Autonomy lies not in being an uncaused cause but in the capacity to "reflectively endorse or reject prompted actions" (p. 1573). | Read |
| [NOTE-442](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-442.md) | Self-determination theory and the facilitation of intrinsic motivation, social development, and well-being | SDT's canonical short statement. Social contexts that support competence, autonomy and relatedness sustain intrinsic motivation and let people internalize and integrate extrinsic regulations; controlling, rejecting or overchallenging contexts undermine intrinsic motivation and leave regulations external or introjected. Autonomy is graded: four kinds of extrinsic motivation lie on a continuum of relative autonomy (Ryan & Connell's quasi-simplex). Basic needs are defined by their consequences for well-being, and need-deprivation is offered as a principal source of distress and psychopathology. | Read |
| [NOTE-443](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-443.md) | Précis of Breakdown of Will | Hyperbolic discounting makes preference reverse with delay alone, so a person is a population of interests that forestall one another. The same recursion predicts legalism, "lapse districts", motivated misperception and compulsive over-control, and premature satiation of appetite limits what will can do for emotional reward. | Read |
| [NOTE-453](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-453.md) | Evolution of the Internal Family Systems Model | Schwartz's short statement of the IFS model. | [NOTE-457](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-457.md) | Internal Family Systems Therapy | Chapter 1 only. Schwartz tells how IFS grew out of structural and strategic family therapy. Clients with bulimia described warring "parts". Coercing parts made matters worse, and curiosity revealed that they protected the client. When interfering parts were asked to "step back", a calm, compassionate "Self" appeared that needed no development. The chapter ends with eight essentials: ecological respect for protectors, Self-leadership, unblending, attention to polarizations, non-pathologizing burdens, movement between system levels, and innate self-healing. | Skimmed |
| [NOTE-460](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-460.md) | Précis: Being No One | Metzinger's own sketch of the self-model theory. | [NOTE-470](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-470.md) | “First we invented stories, then they changed us”: The Evolution of Narrative Identity | McAdams's review essay on narrative identity: "the internalized and evolving story a person invents to explain how he or she has become the person he or she is becoming". | [NOTE-488](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-488.md) | Conscious birds | Review.
